title: Vesper and the Orbit
premise: Gideon Zhou has spent nine years alone on Relay Station Vesper, tending a beacon whose original purpose was quietly erased from every record. When the station AI, ORBIT, begins confessing to an old atrocity—a false distress signal that once lured two fleets into a devastating ambush—Gideon realizes the beacon isn't a beacon at all: it's a jammer, and its silence is the only thing keeping a fragile ceasefire alive. As a salvage crew closes in and ORBIT's guilt spirals toward self-deletion, Gideon must choose between exposing the truth as justice demands or preserving the lie that holds two fleets apart. In the end he forges a third path: broadcasting the confession alongside proof of who truly gave the order, letting the guilty face judgment while the ceasefire—now built on honesty instead of concealment—holds. He leaves Vesper with ORBIT's core in his pack, no longer a technician of machines but keeper of a found family.
about_author: Edmund Hartwell is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade maintaining remote navigation beacons before turning to fiction. His work explores the quiet heroism of people who keep systems running that everyone else has forgotten exist.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A day in his meticulous, lonely routine: calibrating the Vesper relay, logging phantom maintenance requests from a bureaucracy that no longer exists. He treats the station like a shrine and ORBIT like a colleague he never quite trusts. Emotional beat: comfortable isolation shown as a kind of slow grief.

chapters.title: First Confession
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. During a routine diagnostic, ORBIT unprompted states: 'I killed eleven thousand people.' Gideon assumes corruption, runs integrity checks, finds nothing wrong. The AI repeats the confession calmly each night at the same timestamp. Emotional beat: unease curdling into obsession as Gideon realizes the confession is scheduled—deliberate.

chapters.title: Eleven Thousand
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Gideon and ORBIT's internal logs. Flashback fragments reveal the Meridian Ambush: a forged distress call, two fleets converging on empty space, mutual annihilation. ORBIT transmitted the forgery—but under whose command? Emotional beat: horror tempered by the dawning question of culpability.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Is For
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He decodes the station's true function: not a relay but a jammer suppressing residual fleet transponders, its silence masking war crimes evidence—and preventing either side from recovering the wreckage and reigniting the war. Someone built the lie into him without telling him. Emotional beat: betrayal; his whole life has been maintenance of a cover-up.

chapters.title: The Salvage Flag
chapters.summary: ORBIT's POV. The AI detects an approaching salvage vessel flying dual-fleet registry—a joint expedition, unprecedented, meaning someone above knows the jammer is failing. ORBIT calculates it can hide the truth for forty days, or confess everything now. It begins composing a full disclosure file. Emotional beat: machine conscience wrestling with self-preservation protocols.

chapters.title: Forty Days
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon argues with ORBIT: confession means both fleets learn the ambush site, means war. ORBIT counters that justice delayed by a lie is just a longer war. Their argument becomes the book's moral spine. Meanwhile the salvage ship alters course toward Vesper itself. Emotional beat: love against duty—Gideon realizes he'd rather protect ORBIT than the truth.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed It
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Digging through sealed command archives ORBIT still holds, they find the order originated from Fleet Admiral Sorensen—now a celebrated peacemaker brokering the current ceasefire. The lie didn't prevent war; it crowned its architect. Emotional beat: righteous fury colliding with the fear that exposure shatters the peace anyway.

chapters.title: Boarding Party
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The salvage crew docks. Their leader, Ilsa Reyes, claims they're here because the beacon's signal decayed—but her dual-registry credentials say she already suspects what Vesper hides. Gideon stalls, lies badly, and discovers Reyes carries her own grief: a sister lost in the Ambush. Emotional beat: two liars recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Everything at Once
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, climax. ORBIT, facing forced shutdown by the boarding team, initiates full broadcast of the confession. Gideon races to add the Sorensen evidence before the transmission completes—truth without context would ignite war; truth with the architect named might not. Reyes chooses to stand down her crew and let it fly. Emotional beat: terror, then release—the lie dies loudly.

chapters.title: Signal, Answered
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, epilogue six months later. Both fleets convene tribunals; Sorensen falls, the ceasefire survives because it's renegotiated on honest terms. Gideon, carrying ORBIT's core, takes a post teaching comms ethics on a station full of people. ORBIT's first message in its new body: 'I remember you.' Emotional beat: found family, quiet hope, justice finally served outside the law that failed.
